P01.passage: A woolen mill stood on a hill trout stream from 1840 until 1930, and the next year a fisheries officer walked the stream from source to river. Its wheel turned in the open current, and the whole stream ran past it. The mill rinsed its dyed wool in that current, and for two miles below, the water stained a jar blue, held no trout or insect larvae, and left a blue rim on the gravel bars and alder roots along both banks. Above the mill, trout were as many as in the next valley's streams. His report judged that in ninety years the mill had ______ the stream.
P01.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P02.passage: For a decade the old salt mine served the nearby city's art museum as its ______. The mine's chambers lie six hundred feet down, where the air stays cool and dry all year, and a single lift shaft reaches them. While the museum's building was rebuilt, its paintings went down the shaft in sealed crates, which were stacked unopened behind steel doors, with guards who let no one in. When the new building opened, every crate went back up, and each canvas was found exactly as it had been packed.
P02.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P03.passage: From 1400 to 1700 a monastery stood on a ledge above the only road through a mountain valley, and its account books survive. Each year more of its income came from wine and beer sold to drovers and merchants on the road than from its fields, and its few beds were let by the night. In plague years it closed its gate and sold through a hatch in the wall. Its library was a dozen books, all bought in the city, and it kept no money overnight, sending each week's takings down to the bishop. In those books, one historian has argued, the monastery appears as the valley's ______.
P03.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P04.passage: In 1890 a novel about a fishing family on a bleak northern coast, written in a small country's language, appeared in its first English translation. The translator moved the story to a village on the English coast, turned its fjord into an estuary and its money into shillings, and gave every character an English name. He kept every chapter, and every drowning and every winter of hunger is told in full. Set beside the original line by line, the translation shows that its translator ______ the novel. His sentences follow the original's short, abrupt rhythm clause by clause.
P04.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P05.passage: One spring the river rose over its banks and stood on a farmer's lowest field for nine days. The water came down brown from logged hills and, once the river fell, drained off the field's sandy loam, leaving two inches of bark chips, leaves and straw. Corn planted on schedule into the damp soil under that layer stayed green through a midsummer drought that wilted the higher field, and the usual early-summer weeds hardly showed. Walking the field in late summer, the county's soil scientist said that the flood had ______ it. Her samples showed the same nitrogen in the top foot of soil as before the flood.
P05.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P06.passage: Beside a rail line, a strip of uncut grass a few yards wide runs twelve miles across plowed farmland between two forests, and meadow voles live in both forests. Two decades of trapping suggest that the strip has served as the voles' ______. Marked voles from the forest edges are caught in the strip after dark, among grass stems clipped of their seed heads, and back at the forest edge by morning; none has been caught more than a few hundred yards from the forest it came from. They nest only in the forests, and voles that visit the strip outlive, on average, voles that never leave the forest.
P06.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P07.passage: A city turned a forty-acre rail yard into a park, with a highway on its north edge and, to the south, row houses and apartment towers that the yard had divided for a century. Its lawns and a concert shell slope open to the highway, and new restaurants now line the streets facing its gates. Gate counts found most visitors arriving by train or car from beyond the district and staying three hours, with row-house and tower residents a tenth of the crowd. A study of the park's first decade called it the district's ______. Rents on its south edge doubled over those years.
P07.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P08.passage: Two geologists measured the stones of a steep river running eight miles from granite and sandstone cliffs to the sea. Their report argued that the river had ______ those stones, and its photographs set out the case. Sieved, the bed held the same mix of sizes at the cliffs as at the sea. Painted stones moved a mile downstream with each flood, lying wherever they stopped. A stone cracked open showed the same shade inside as out. Every stone, boulder to pebble, was rounded to the hand, and the spring floods that roll them leave the river gray with fine grit.
P08.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P09.passage: A two-lane road laid across a valley floor in 1960 carried loaded logging trucks for thirty years, and surveyors checked it each fall against stakes along its shoulders. Each July its asphalt softened in the heat, and the trucks, keeping to the same wheel tracks on the narrow lanes, pressed it down a little more every summer, most on the long climb where they crawled in low gear. The stakes showed the roadbed at the height it was laid, and the asphalt at the stop sign below the climb, where trucks braked hard, never cracked or shifted. By 1990, its surface had been ______.
P09.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P10.passage: In 1960 a dam was built across a mountain river, holding back a reservoir three hundred feet deep. Twenty years of surveys show that the dam has ______ the river below it. Its turbines draw water from near the reservoir's floor and pass it through at an even rate, day and night, and each May the snowmelt flood still pours over the spillway and rolls the gravel bars below as it always has. The stretch below the dam, once thick with bass, now holds almost none; trout spawn instead on gravel bars lying as deep under water as before 1960, and the bass have retreated to reaches thirty miles downstream.
P10.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P11.passage: For two centuries a flock of sheep has grazed one slope of a narrow valley in the hills, while a stone wall along the stream has kept them off the opposite slope. The flock keeps to narrow tracks running level across its slope, each a foot below the next, like the treads of a stair, worn to bare earth by hooves. Between the tracks the grass grows as rough and tall as across the stream, and its soil tests no richer than the ungrazed slope's. Comparing the two slopes, one ecologist concluded that the flock had ______ its hillside.
P11.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P12.passage: In 1690 a merchant ship carrying iron bars and wine sank in sixty feet of water off a rocky coast. The water at that depth stays near freezing and so low in oxygen that the boring worms of warmer coasts cannot live there. Divers in 1990 found the hull upright on the open bottom where it settled, its masts standing, its carved stern still showing red paint, ropes coiled on its deck and wine in its casks. The divers' report says that three centuries of seawater had ______ the ship. Its oak, brought up, was hard enough to take a nail.
P12.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P13.passage: In 1990 conservators began a ten-year survey of a ruined castle wall, half of which had been cloaked in ivy for two centuries. Behind the ivy the mortar had long since crumbled to sand, and the plant's woody stems, thick as a wrist, wove through and around the loose stones. Moisture readings in the stone behind the leaves matched those on the bare half, and stone faces under the stems were clean. The survey's final report says that the ivy had ______ the wall. When a gale in the survey's eighth year brought down forty feet of the bare half, the ivy-covered half stood.
P13.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P14.passage: In 1790 a merchant ship carrying iron bars and casks of wine sank in thirty feet of water off a sandy coast that storms strike every winter. Two centuries on the seabed had ______ the ship, according to the divers who surveyed it in 1990. Its hull still lies where it settled, its outline unbroken on open sand that the current sweeps clean, in warm water where shipworms thrive. A plank the divers raised, smooth and pale on its surface, was as light as cork and crumbled in their hands.
P14.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P15.passage: In 1911 a steel freighter struck a reef off a small island and sank, and its hull still lies there, nearly whole. Divers who surveyed it in 2005 called the hull a true ______, and their photographs show why. It carried sixty chests of silver coins, and its sealed holds kept salvors out until 1985, when divers cut through and found every chest where the manifest placed it. Its crew were taken off by a passing schooner the next morning. It lies in eighty feet of murky water, its plates furred with silt, far below the keels of passing ships.
P15.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P16.passage: A lone coral outcrop the size of a small car rises from the sand of a shallow lagoon, a quarter mile inside the reef that rings it. For a few nights after the first full moon of summer, groupers from reefs up to thirty miles away crowd around it by the thousand, and swarms of small fish gather among them. At dusk the males turn dark and circle the larger females. Within a week the groupers are gone, and females caught there on the last night weigh a fifth less than females caught on the first. Divers who have logged its visitors since 1985 call the outcrop the lagoon's ______.
P16.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P17.passage: In 1590 a printer issued an engraved chart of a stretch of coast, copied from a navy surveyor's hand-drawn map. The print is the survey's size, north is at the top of both, and every cape, bay, and shoal sits where the survey puts it. Across the open water, which the surveyor left blank, the engraver added spouting whales and a galleon under full sail, and the title, plain lettering on the survey, sits in a scrolled frame laid with gold leaf. Setting the two side by side, a historian found that the engraver had ______ the survey.
P17.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P18.passage: When wolves returned to a mountain valley in 1995, a pack of nine settled along the creek where a herd of four hundred elk spends each winter. Over the decade that followed, the pack ______ the herd. The wolves spent their days bedded in the willow thickets beside the crossings where the elk came down each evening to drink, and nearly every carcass lay within a few yards of the thickets' edge, most of the elk struck there falling within three strides. The herd went on using the same crossings, and the willows around them stayed browsed to knee height.
P18.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P19.passage: From 1952 to 1957 almost no rain fell on a pine forest in the southern hills, where foresters measured every tree yearly until 1975. Through every dry summer the needles of every pine turned brown by August and dropped weeks early, and each spring the trees grew a full set of new ones. The few pines that died, large and small alike, stayed standing for years until they rotted. Once the rains returned, growth rings were as wide as they had been before 1952, and bark beetles, which attack weakened pines, found few hosts. The foresters' final report concluded that the dry years had ______ the forest.
P19.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P20.passage: In 1902 a woman published the prairie diary her mother had kept from 1858 to 1871, and the mother's notebooks now sit in a state archive. Scholars who set the book beside the notebooks in 1990 found that the daughter had ______ the diary. Every entry is there, in the notebooks' order, and nothing in the book comes from outside them. The book is a third shorter: the weekly egg tallies and the daily notes on the wind are gone. The curses the mother wrote after quarrels with her husband are printed whole, misspellings like "chickins" and "sumer" included.
P20.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P21.passage: For thirty years beavers have lived on a creek in a dry mountain valley; the creek in the next valley has none. Their dams have backed the creek into a chain of ponds that cover the old meadow four feet deep, drowning the pines there, and silt settling out of the still water raises the pond floors each year. The beavers build with willows from the banks, which sprout again each spring, and the aspens on the slopes stand as thick as in the next valley. A hydrologist who has studied both valleys concludes that the beavers have ______ theirs. In dry summers both valleys turn the same brown.
P21.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P22.passage: In 1760 a riverside landowner built a brick wall twelve feet high and a quarter mile long beside his orchard, near a village of thatched cottages. It runs along the orchard's northern edge, between the trees and the cottages, open at both ends, and the river lies a mile to the south. When spring frost blackens the blossom, it blackens every tree, those beside the wall too. A fire in 1791 burned every cottage to the ground, and the orchard lost only the scorched leaves of its nearest row. Estate letters of the next fifty years treat the wall as the orchard's ______.
P22.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P23.passage: On one island a thorny shrub with hollow thorns and nectar glands houses ants on nearly every plant. For three years an ecologist kept the ants off some shrubs with sticky bands and compared them with their neighbors. Banded shrubs flowered, podded and grew as well as their neighbors, and caterpillars chewed both alike. In those three years, the ants ______ the shrub. Their seeds, each tipped with a small oily knob, lay where they dropped until mice found them, while seeds falling from the neighbors were gone within a day, and the island's young shrubs stood on ant nest mounds fifty yards from any parent.
P23.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P24.passage: In 1987 a forty-ton whale died at sea and sank two miles to a seafloor where food is otherwise scarce. A biologist who has filmed it since 1988 calls the carcass the seafloor's ______. Within days of its landing, hundreds of sleeper sharks, hagfish and crabs from miles around had crowded onto it, and in four months they had stripped its flesh, leaving bones that bacteria finished within a year. The scavengers are animals found across the whole seafloor, and they scattered as soon as the flesh was gone.
P24.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P25.passage: Twice a day the tide floods a salt marsh where a farm creek meets a bay, then drains it through one channel. For two years a team compared the water leaving by that channel with the water that had entered. It came in brown with mud and left clear, while the marsh floor rose a quarter inch a year. It carried all the creek's fertilizer nitrate on into the bay, feeding the usual summer algae blooms. The team's report calls the marsh the bay's ______. Nearby shrimp were full of plankton, and when the bay's deep water runs short of oxygen in late summer, so does the marsh's outflow.
P25.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P26.passage: Every spring until 1914, the people of one moorland village set out together at dawn, crossed six miles of open common to its far edge, and came home by dusk. At six stopping places along the way, villagers in borrowed armor and painted masks acted out scenes from the village's history, while carriages from the market town followed, scattering the grazing ponies, to watch at a shilling a head. Folklorists who recorded the walk in 1900 called it the village's yearly ______. The last scene, played at the boundary stone, showed the village beating off an attack from the neighboring parish in 1460.
P26.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P27.passage: In 1851 a young poet paid a printer in her city to issue three hundred copies of her first collection, on terms that gave her a share of every copy sold. Within months each city paper had reviewed the collection by printing her name over its weakest stanza, quoted in full beside a cartoon of a weeping cow, with no comment at all. Her printer, who held the only plates, sold forty copies and let the rest go as scrap paper. Within two years, her poems had been ______.
P27.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P28.passage: During a two-year war in the 1870s, one small country's government changed how it dealt with the country's four daily newspapers. A new war tax on each copy sold tripled the price of a paper, and within a year circulation had halved. Two of the four dailies closed, and the two that survived let go half their reporters. Both stayed in private hands and printed whatever they pleased. One historian's account of those years says the government ______ the press. Among the things the two survivors pleased to print were weekly attacks on the tax and on the war.
P28.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P29.passage: A clay tablet dug from the ruins of an ancient river city lists barley in nine lines, each giving an amount followed by a word or two, and a seal has been rolled across its back. Each line pairs a man's name with the barley he was given that month, the amounts cut by a fixed share for two names marked as boys, and the seal is the temple overseer's. The tablet lay in the temple storeroom among eleven others like it, one for each month of that year, all with the same nine names. Scholars now read the tablet as its owner's ______.
P29.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P30.passage: For three summers an entomologist watched garden ants tend aphids on a row of beans, lapping up the honeydew the aphids release. Aphids on leaves a worker had crossed crept a third as fast as on clean leaves, and fewer grew the wings aphids need to leave a plant. The aphids stayed on whatever shoot they had settled on, wilting or not, in clusters that grew all summer until the first frost killed them on the stems. Her report concludes that the ants had ______ the aphids. On a row the ants could not reach, aphids scattered within days, and by midsummer it held three times as many.
P30.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P31.passage: Twenty thousand years ago a glacier half a mile thick filled a mountain valley, and it lay there for several thousand years. The ice was frozen fast to the ground beneath it, and the soil of the valley's meadows survived under it, still holding pollen older than the ice. When it melted, boulders of a dark basalt found nowhere in the valley, some as large as houses, settled across the meadows, each resting on that old soil. That glacier, geologists agree, ______ the valley floor. Today the river wanders between the boulders in a shallow, stony bed.
P31.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P32.passage: In 1789 a fleet of eleven sailing ships left port carrying settlers along a coast of sandy bays and rocky headlands. In its third week at sea, the weather ______ several of the fleet's ships. A fog rolled in so thick that a lookout on the bow of one could not make out its own stern, while a steady breeze kept every ship moving at its usual speed. Ships fired guns every few minutes to keep their places, and two that strayed from the line passed within yards of rocks they never saw, reaching harbor afloat and unharmed.
P32.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P33.passage: In 1859 a merchant built a log store at a mountain gold camp, the only building there with a stove, an iron safe and a shelf of bottles, and his ledger survives. When fever swept the camp in the summer of 1860, he dosed miners from the bottles with quinine and laudanum by weights copied from a physician's handbook, and the ledger charges each man by the dose, to be paid from his next cleanup. One historian of the camp called the store, in those years, the camp's ______. He kept the laudanum locked in the safe beside his takings and barred the door at sundown.
P33.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P34.passage: In 1797 an occupying army entered a port city whose museum held some four hundred paintings and bronzes, many of them carried off from neighboring towns by the city's own fleet a century earlier. On the first night soldiers broke open the cases and filled their packs with coins, cameos and the smaller bronzes, leaving slashed canvases on the floor. Nothing was listed, and over the next decade pieces surfaced in shops across the army's home country, sold by men discharged from its ranks; the council, asked for nothing, got nothing back. Within a year, the army had ______ the museum's collection.
P34.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P35.passage: A glacier fills the head of a high valley whose river runs past farming villages to the plain. It can be seen only from the last village, where the road from the plain ends. Snow piles on it all winter, and the river runs fullest at the height of summer, when the plain's rain-fed streams dry up and the villages open their ditches. Its meltwater filters for days through gravel, so the river's level hardly changes between morning and night. Its front has held one rock ledge since the 1700s, through warm decades and cold. A study of three centuries of village records describes the glacier as the valley's ______.
P35.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P36.passage: When wolves returned to a mountain valley in 1996, biologists began counting its one elk herd each winter and tracking collared elk year-round. Over the following decade, the wolves ______ the herd. By 2006 the river meadows held as many elk in winter as ever, and the collared cows kept to their old ranges. Filmed there, an elk now raised its head every few seconds, fed a third less of each hour than elk filmed before 1996, and bolted at a raven's call, while the few elk the wolves took were mostly first-winter calves, so the herd grew older and its total barely changed.
P36.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P37.passage: A sandbar lies across the river mouth below the old port, twelve feet under water at high tide and bare at low tide. Harbor records from the 1800s show the bar serving as the port's ______ for most of a century. Every ship drawing over six feet waited outside for high water and took aboard a town-licensed bar pilot, who guided ships over three or four at a time for a fee the council set; those fees paved the town's streets. Once across, ships tied up at the town's piers to unload, and in winter gales the ocean swells rolled over the bar and broke against those piers.
P37.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P38.passage: In the second year of the war, the northern alliance ______ the island's only port. Before the war the port had shipped wool to buyers on both sides of the strait. Alliance warships stood off the harbor through the spring, and by summer the southern alliance's coal depot on the quay was a crater and the waterfront sheds beside it were rubble. In the weeks between attacks freighters of every flag still came and went, the island's wool still sold in the alliance's markets, and the island's flag went on flying over the roofless customs house.
P38.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P39.passage: In 1951 the last congregation left a stone church that had stood at the center of a river town since 1720. Engineers that winter found its walls sound and its tower true. Over the next year workers took it down stone by stone, painting a number on each, and a college across the ocean that had paid the town for it raised it again on its own lawn, where it stands today. The square where it had stood became a garden. The town's minutes record that in 1952 the council ______ the church.
P39.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P40.passage: For two centuries after 1700, the dunes of a desert basin pressed against a walled oasis village of mud-brick houses and date palms. Wind slowing in the still air behind its walls dropped a few inches of sand into its lanes and gardens each year. Families kept every house by laying new floors over the sand and building fresh rooms and doorways on top. A well dug in the village's main lane passes through thirty feet of sand and floors to reach the first street, all inside the same circuit of walls. Caravans climb a ramp to the eastern gate. In those two centuries, the sand had ______ the village.
P40.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
